utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. And good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, you may recall that when we adjourned on Friday we were reviewing the interview of March 24th, 1991, which is 65 ter 25195.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could call that up again, please, and turn to page 7 of the English and page 61 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, we had previously looked at an excerpt that immediately preceded the one I'm going to turn you to, that was the question about whether Europe was going to observe it calmly and your response concerning Europe's unwillingness to go to war. And then the passage continues. The questioner asks: "You believe that the Serbian people are ready to go to war?" And your response was: "I believe that, with their genetic code, the Serbian people are always ready to go to war." And you continue: "Every Serb is born as a soldier, and even Europe knows it." Did that accurately reflect your position on the -- what you regarded as the position of the Serbian people and their leadership in connection with the options available in the event that events took a turn contrary to the objectives or interests of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with any kind of position of the Serbian leadership. This is just my personal position and perhaps the position of the political party that I belong to. You see, sir, this interview goes beyond the time of Mr. Karadzic's indictment, even beyond the time of the indictment issued against me. So this is my constant opinion, my view of the world, my view of the Serbian people, and so on, and that is the truth. However, the Serb people is a very unhappy people too or very unlucky. They did not have a good leadership when Yugoslavia started disintegrating. They put their trust up the JNA that was not up to the historical challenges of that time, and the Serb people were seriously divided by internal rifts dating back to the Second World War, the division between the Partizans and the Chetniks. This is a very tragic division that caused a great deal of trouble amongst the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I also -- excuse me, I also want to ask you about the next passage where the questioner asks: "Can one reach a solution with cool heads and with rifles laid down?" And your response was: "How is one supposed to negotiate with the Ustashas? Did you see today that the Croatian people are entirely Ustasha? There are very few exceptions." And then you go on to give credit and honour to the residents of Istria, Rijeka, and Kvarner. Did that reflect your view at the time about the extent of the Ustasha philosophy among the Croatian people? And secondly, since you mention the time-period, did that position change over time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is not about Ustasha philosophy. There is no such thing. This is Ustasha ideology, which is clerofascistic; clero because it fully includes the Roman Catholic church in Croatia as supported by the Vatican throughout, and also they wanted to build a theocracy, and it's fascist because it is not based so much on the Italian fascist regime under Mussolini but rather Germany's regime under Hitler. Actually, in practice the Ustasha ideology outdid the Hitler regime, Hitler had an industry of killing, whereas the Croats in the Second World War loved killing, enjoyed killing. These are two rather different things. From the point of view of this time perspective, perhaps that is not important for the victims involved, but at that time it was easier for a victim that was killed in an easy way, not involving great suffering or without being subjected to torture. Within the Ustasha Independent State of Croatia, people were not killed before being terribly tortured beforehand. So first of all, let us see what this is. It is not a philosophy, it is an ideology. Franjo Tudjman is an advocate of that ideology. First of all, he proved that in his book. It was called "Bespuca Povijesne Zbiljnosti." He quoted the Bible, also the Old Testament, trying to justify genocide. Already in the 1980s he announced that he was dreaming of a new genocide, and then when he took power in Croatia, then he first stated that the Independent State of Croatia, this clerofascist creation from the Second World War, was an expression of the historical aspirations of the Croatian people for statehood. And this was even included in the preamble of the new constitution of Croatia. I think that it was passed in December 1990. This regime openly declared itself as an Ustasha regime, and this regime did not exactly win a majority of votes in the election. As far as I can remember, it was about 48 per cent. However, after having fully taken over all the reins of power, he created this amazing euphoria among the Croatian people and a vast, enormous majority of Croats followed that regime and his Ustasha ideology. Of course there are exceptions and I respect these exceptions. There are honourable and honest Croats who realised what a lethal ideology that was even at the time. Actually, if you look at this historically, ethnically, and linguistically, these are actually true Croats from Istria, from the Dalmatian islands. These are Croats who have still preserved the Croatian language, at least as their local dialect, Chakavian. Our greatest problem were those Croats, who are originally Serb, who became Catholics and then tried to prove that they were greater Catholics than the pope as it were. They were artificially incorporated in the Croatian national corpus and they hated the most those that they originated from; that is to say, the Orthodox Serbs because deep down in their hearts they know that they originate from these same Orthodox Serbs. So this is the second part of my response to your question. The third part, Franjo Tudjman immediately after taking over started resorting openly to Ustasha methods. Serbs were persecuted, dismissed from work, especially from government jobs. They were compelled to seek these so-called Domovnicas; that is to say, they had to have documents issued to them stating that they were loyal citizens of the Croatian state. He started taking away their apartments, persecuting intellectuals. Many Serbs were beaten up. All of this was done with a view to making it impossible for them to live peacefully in the territory of the former Croatian federal unit. The Serbs felt what was going to happen, that is why there was this great unrest, restlessness, and I was aware of all these dangers that were there because of Tudjman's coming to power. So to this day basically this is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last passage in this particular interview that I'd like to ask you about is found at page 12 and page 65 -- page 12 in the English, and page 65 in the Serbian. And the question was asked: "Finally, where is the end to everything that is happening to us in the Balkans?" And you stated: "It is in the renewal of a free and independent Serbian state in the Balkans, encompassing all Serbian territories, meaning in addition to the present-day federal unit of Serbia proper, also Serbian Macedonia, Serbian Montenegro, Serbian Bosnia, Serbian Herzegovina ..." et cetera, as we see in the remainder of the passage. Again, Dr. Seselj, was that an accurate reflection of your view of the -- what the overall objective was and more specifically what constituted the territories of the Serbian state that should be established with all the territories?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my general objective, not the general objective of Serbia or the then-Yugoslavia or the Serbian leadership or other political parties. This is the programme objective of the Serb Radical Party. We openly presented it in our programme when we established the party. This is in the document founding the party, so no other political party had an identical objective. So I am striving for the exclusiveness of this political objective. Now, what stands behind this? First of all, even before political parties were established in the then-Yugoslavia, I publicly advocated allowing Slovenia to secede from Yugoslavia. Slovenes did not want to live in Yugoslavia. Why would we keep them there by force? If they wish independence, then they could achieve independence and Serbian policy had to be in favour of them and had to allow them to leave. Ethnically it's a rather homogenous state, Slovenia. There are no border issues that were unresolved and they could leave if that was the will of the Slovenian people. Croats could also leave but not by taking away parts of Serb territory with them because the Croatian federal unit after the Second World War was established with the proclaimed consent of Croats and Serbs living within its boundaries, stating that that was their federal unit. The Serb right of a constituent people in the territory of Dalmatia, Croatia, and Slavonia dates back to 1881, as far back as that, at the time when the Vojna Krajina, the military Krajina, was established. That is an area where Austria brought Serbs for centuries so that these Serbs would defend them from Turks. Serbs enjoyed privileges there, there was no feudalism, there, they were not serfs and so on and so forth. Now, since the Turkish danger was no longer there, since Austria occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Sandzak of Novi Pazar - not fully but they had their barracks there - there was no state reason any longer for the existence of the Vojna Krajina, the military Krajina; however, politicians on the Serb side, on the Croatian side aspired for unity. They thought that if they were united it would be easier for them to oppose the centralist efforts of Vienna and especially of Hungary and they agreed that the Vojna Krajina would be part of Dalmatia, Croatia, and Slavonia; however, that the Serbs would be a constituent people there. Now, I hope that you will bear with me and I hope that you will have enough patience to hear me out. You know what my problem is? For one year and three months I have not been appearing in this courtroom in The Hague, so I could hardly wait for this moment to come. Perhaps I'm a bit too extensive in my answers; however, I hope that you will bear with me, I hope that you will not interrupt me. One of your predecessors did not really fair very well. He was very brazen, very impudent, and I hope that -- and then he got what he had coming to him; however, I hope that you are going to be all right as you have been so far --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If -- if -- thank you. Perhaps we can reach some kind of understanding about that. It's certainly not my intention to cut you off and I appreciate -- what I think what is happening now is that you want to explain the basis for the position that we just read about in that interview and I appreciate the fact that there is a -- that you want to elaborate a very considerable historical basis and with a lot of knowledge about what happened that you want to share with the Court. So I'm looking for a way to shortcut that because there are various other portions of things that you said that I imagine you also want the Court to hear about that I'm trying to get to in the limited time that we have. So I'm trying to indicate to you when I think you've conveyed to the Court what I believe is a sufficient basis for them to understand your position. Of course I leave that up to you. I'm not -- I don't have the power to stop you or the authority, but the Court may also want to ask you to allow an opportunity for further information to be developed. Here, in this instance, I think we've touched on a subject that could be discussed at great length and consume virtually all the time we have. If we could leave it at the fact that this is, if I understand it correctly, your position and that you consider that there are very valid and legitimate historical reasons for that position which you could elaborate at length if there was sufficient time, I would like to move on to the next topic. If you think there is a point or two that really needs to be made in connection with this, that's another matter, but I think the Court understands your view that this is not an arbitrary position but that it is based on history.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the main part of my answer that your question is yet to come. You stated there which territories I consider Serbian. I would like to give you reasons why I consider that for each territory very briefly. You mentioned about a dozen --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I -- I --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was important to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I agree. But I think it would be extremely helpful if we focused on Bosnia and to some extent Croatia since we're touching on that, but primarily Bosnia rather than the other areas. That will certainly be more efficient for us and more focused.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Middle Ages Bosnia was a small dukedom in the east of Serbia. The original Serbia comprised the areas of today's north Albania, today's Montenegro, Zaljune [phoen], Hum, and the Neretva dukedom which is today's Herzegovina. Of course, there were Serbs living outside these borders, but they were under Bulgarian rule and then gradually they liberated themselves from Bulgarian rule. Medieval Bosnia was clearly Serbian and by all Byzantine documents you can see it was Serbian. At the time of the Nemanjics, the so-called Bogumili appeared in Serbia, it was a sect inside the Orthodox church. A Stevan expelled them into the small Bosnian dukedom, and later the pope went into a number of crusades against the Bogumili and the main force in permitting it were the Hungarians. The Serbs who then became Catholics with time, under pressure gave, up their national consciousness. But only at the end of the 19th century they were forced to declare themselves as Croats. There is no document, historical document, showing that they were Croats before that. The Muslims are Serbs who during the Turkish occupation adopted Islam. At the start it meant substantial privileges in society, but later on it was no longer the case. You may have heard of the word "balija." I never used that because it's a condescending term for the Muslims, but the balijas were Muslims who were late in converting to Islam and therefore were unable to get any privileges but remained serfs. Dubrovnik has always been a Serbian town. Initially, that is originally, it was a Roman town, but later on the Serbian population prevailed and Dubrovnik adopted the Serbian language. Dalmatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not interested in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, sir, it's not that I'm not interested, it's not that others aren't interested it's only a matter of time. And with respect, I think you're showing your academic background and providing all the details I presume you would want students of this matter to understand in detail, but I'm sure -- I'm very confident you're more than smart enough to provide us with a summary, capsulisation, a quick response that summarises your position without all the underlying arguments and facts in response to any question like this. So rather than a tutorial on the subject which I know is significant, which I know is vast, we just need as quick an answer as possible. If the answer is: Bosnia was always inhabited by people who were originally Serbs who converted to Islam under some forms of pressure or for advantage, then you can say that. But please, try to get us to the underlying point. Obviously if that specific point is challenged, then you can provide the details that support it, but I trust you will try to avoid the kind of extensive lecture that might be suitable in another context.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the Austro-Hungarian occupation, the ethnic majority were Orthodox Serbs and not Muslim until the genocide of the Serbs in the Second World War. But where did this huge percentage of the Muslim Serbs in Bosnia come from? After the Vienna war, the Muslim Serbs withdrew from Hungary, Slavonia, Lika, and gathered in Bosnia. That is the essence. After the Serbian uprisings in Serbia, the greater part of the Muslim population left the so-called Serbia proper or the Serbian dukedom and settled in Bosnia. That's why a greater concentration of Muslims came about, greater than otherwise, or rather, elsewhere in other countries that were -- or lands that were under Turkish occupation. As for Croatia, it had a territory under the Cetina river, that is in the hinterland of Split, up until the Gvozd mountain. The Croatian historians proved as much. At the time of King Tomislav, the Dalmatian towns from Split to Zadar had a Roman population also were part of Croatia, and at the time of Petar Kresimir the IV, Slavonia also belonged to Croatia but not the Slavonia that -- the capital of which is Osijek but the Slavonia that is actually today's Croatian Zagorje. The Croats fled these territories because the Turks were advancing and they settled in central Europe around Vienna and today's Slovak president, Mr. Gasparovic, is of Croatian descent. And the Austrian settled Serbian population in those empty homes because they wanted reliable defence. We Serbs as a people were divided to such an extent that on the one hand the Christian Serbs defended Austria and on the other hand the Muslim Serbs fought on the side of the Turkish empire in its conquests. Is it a bit clearer to you now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I thank you for that response. As I indicated a little bit more fulsome in detail than I would hope for, but I'm going to move on to some of your other interviews at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those excerpts, Mr. President, and move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes we will receive them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6387, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Seselj, we began on Friday with the March interview during which you mentioned your support for Dr. Karadzic in the SDS in March of 1991. I wanted to turn to another document that appears to reflect your position on the same subject in 1995 and that's 40296. You'll be familiar with that, that's the familiar with Laura Silber for the Death of Yugoslavia documentary. And the relevant excerpt can be found at time code 01:36:44 to 01:38:36 and can also be found at page 26 and 27 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number again, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any appendix?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can read it, I think. This is a videotape that I imagine Dr. Seselj has himself seen before, so -- although I wanted to provide him with an opportunity to see his words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't find anything with that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it has an A at the end, 40296A, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it had to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can play that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Well, what is even more typical, what is interesting perhaps and what I haven't told anyone yet is this: At one time while putting pressure on Karadzic, Milosevic tried to ensure my presence at the Serbian Presidency but so that it would appear unintentional. For example, he was meeting with Karadzic and then they called me and I literally ran into Karadzic at his office door. Or the conversation with Karadzic was ongoing when I arrived, a few polite words were exchanged, and he left as I came in. It's as if he used my presence to lend weight to whatever he said to pressure Karadzic. Of course, after that, I either phone Karadzic or sent a message through some people that this was out of the question, that it was out of the question for me to support any pressure put on him. "Then, Karadzic was genuinely surprised by Milosevic's decision to blockade the Drina border. This was definitely an act of betrayal of high treason, the likes of which has never been seen in all our history. He thought that Milosevic would never do such a thing and he was surprised by it for a few days but he quickly composed himself and opposed it. You know, Karadzic has one advantage in politics that the rest of us don't have, he's a professional psychiatrist. "Well, I can't tell you what Karadzic said to me in confidence. I won't do that because I'm a true friend of Radovan Karadzic as long as he pursues this kind of politics. I will never tell you anything that someone else might use against him or that might put him in an unpleasant situation. What he told me in confidence remains ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stop that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So first with respect to the comments you made we heard at the very end, this interview, as I understand it, took place in March of 1995, is it -- would that reflect the fact that your support for Dr. Karadzic continued into that time-period and that this accurately reflected your position about Dr. Karadzic and your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict between Milosevic and Karadzic has -- had been going on latently from the first elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990 when the Serb Democratic Party got the majority of votes of the Serbian people and shared power with the SDA, the Muslim party, and the HDZ, the Croatian party. The conflict was basically idealogical as far as I know. Mr. Karadzic, who did not favour communism, at least not at that time, you could even say I don't know if he will agree that he was also a kind of an anti-communist, and Milosevic was still a prisoner of the communist world view. He had in principle embraced democratic principles and the reorganisation of the state but he still was inclined to leftist ideas and that sort of tradition. I was on the -- I sided with Mr. Karadzic in their conflict. That doesn't mean that I idealise him. I had a lot to hold against him and I did, but I kept silent over some things to protect the higher interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, you mentioned that in connection with your conflict that you mentioned the ideology of communism. You've previously stated though in addition to whatever friction that caused that Milosevic didn't like Karadzic's nationalism and that was part of the tensions between them as well, at least as I understand it from what you've stated, and I believe you stated it in this very interview?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the sources of conflict between them, but there were others too. Milosevic pretended to be the leader of the entire Serbian people and Mr. Karadzic rose to a great popularity in a short time, and Milosevic didn't want anybody to be more popular than he was, and so on. Those are the small weaknesses that we all have to some extent; that is, each of us hides that more or less successfully. At any rate, the tensions between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Karadzic were ongoing, they never stopped. What affected me most was Milosevic's blockade of the RS. I then turned against Milosevic with all means, I never -- I never picked my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's the translation finally trickling in. At the same time, I understand that despite your dismay over the actions that Mr. Milosevic took in connection with the blockade and the tensions over the Vance-Owen Plan, that you were still willing to give credit where credit was due. I know that you considered and you made clear that you considered support for the Bosnian Serbs and the Serbs in RSK an important and patriotic responsibility, and you gave credit to Milosevic for the things he did do for the RS and the RSK prior to the time of, for example, the blockade, stating again in this interview that Milosevic provided a great deal of help. And, in fact, one can only wonder where RS and RSK would have been without the help that he provided.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Milosevic really provided a great deal of help without the help of Serbia, neither the RS nor the RSK would have been able to survive probably, but one thing is giving help, another thing is assisting crimes. We see that the ICTY acquitted General Perisic through whom all the military help was provided as well as Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic, who also provided help. Whoever was in power in Belgrade had to or would have had to assist the western Serbs like their leaders or not. We know that Milosevic established the socialist party of the RS to oppose the SDS of Mr. Karadzic. In 1993 there was an attempt of a coup d'etat at Banja Luka. I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the interpreters were not able to catch up with your speed, so could you repeat from 1993, attempt of a coup d'etat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was an attempt of a putsch, not a coup d'etat, in Banja Luka in September 1993. When that happened, I went to the speaker's desk of the National Assembly and openly attacked the military security service, then the League of Communists, the movement for Yugoslavia, and one of Milosevic's ministers as the organisers. The League of Communists, the movement for Yugoslavia was a party which had some relations with Milosevic because Milosevic's wife was among the leaders of that party. They didn't really like Milosevic much because they were extreme communists. It was the so-called generals' party. You heard of its establishment in 1990. The military security service which was also involved and whose target Mr. Karadzic always was and how did the SPS, Milosevic's party, react? They issued a press release in which they called me a criminal, an alcoholic, and a leftist. Okay. Call me a criminal, a war criminal, I can take that. But how can I be an alcoholic, given that I hardly ever drink alcohol. Nobody can really call me an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I think you've answered that aspect of the question. Can I turn then to, since you've mentioned various organs of -- connected to Mr. Milosevic to some of the concrete examples of support that were discussed in the Death of Yugoslavia interview and let me see if I can put those together and ask you about those. So the first one is found at page 10 of the English and it's at 00:37:40 to 39:56. I'm sorry, for the benefit of the record the clip ended the 01:38:41.4, that's the previous clip we saw.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "When you received those weapons, did that -- you said that in the regime that the regime gave weapons to your party, I mean the volunteers. Was that in -- with the political leaderships with Milosevic's knowledge or through the police and through Vojislav Seselj? "This was this was all done with Milosevic's knowledge, there is no doubt about that. And the key people in the police with whom we co-operated at the time were Radmilo Bogdanovic, Mihalj Kertes, and others; Franko Simatovic, aka Frenki, who later commanded the Red Berets; from the General Staff, we mostly co-operated with General Domazetovic, who was the deputy chief of the General Staff and also at that time the head of the personnel administration, if I remember correctly. There were also contacts with lower-ranking officers and so on depending on the need and the situation. Our volunteers came to Belgrade, the barracks in Bubanj Potok. That is where we put on uniforms and where they were given weapons and buses to take them where they wanted. They were under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army as soon as the Yugoslav People's Army became involved in the fighting. Until the battle in Borovo Selo, the Yugoslav People's Army actually only protected the Croats when it was apparent that they would lose a battle because they still thought that Yugoslavia could be preserved. Until then, our weapons had come only from the police; however, when Tudjman began to blockade the barracks, attack the Yugoslav People's Army, kill officers and soldiers, and so on, that is when the Yugoslav People's Army became involved in the clashes. That is when we had a lot more weapons at our disposal and all our volunteers fell under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army, always where the situation was the most difficult because they were the most disciplined and the bravest. They were -- they went where army units were badly organised, untrained, and ineffective. This was especially obvious during the battle for Vukovar because the army started out with great power, with heavy weapons, and destroyed Vukovar, but it didn't manage to achieve anything. Then they remembered that the town could not be liberated or conquered in this manner so they engaged our volunteer units to literally go street by street and liberate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Another related clip found at page 16, 17 of the English and 00 -- this ends -- sorry, and this clip ended at 00:39:57.1. Now if we could go to 00:58:09 for a short clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Yes. Our volunteers were in Zvornik, Arkan's volunteers were also involved, and there was another formation there belonging to Zuco who was under the command of the police and is now being tried for war crimes. "How did this -- all this unfold? How did you decide to go? Where -- were you were given an order from Belgrade? Were you asked by the Serbian? How did it all happen? "Vojislav Seselj: Yes, we were never given orders. We were always asked, Milosevic asked us, Radmilo Bogdanovic asked us, some general, Domazetovic, for example, or someone else said we need this many volunteers for such and such a place and we gathered the volunteers needed. When they said that they needed the most experienced men, we took the most experienced. When they said those who are inexperienced are acceptable because it is not very dangerous, then we sent the others. This is the way it always happened. "The reporter: Who was it at that time who asked you to send units, was it? "Vojislav Seselj: It was in May 1992. That's when I began to meet with Milosevic frequently and each time Milosevic himself asked for volunteers to be sent. It's not like we needed a lot of convincing. We saw it as our duty, our obligation. It was only with regard to the deployment where they were needed the most because they had the reputation of being the bravest, the most capable, and the most disciplined."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And one more related clip at 1:05:25. And that's found at page 18 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The reporter: The same way you described why this is important for the Serbs, and if you describe could you tell us what happened when you headed to Zvornik, who told you to go, how did this happen? "Vojislav Seselj: Well, in May 1992 Milosevic finally took absolute control over the Yugoslav People's Army. This is when a new constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was declared and when he formally actually and inherently became the main person in the state, the man who decides everything. This Zvornik operation too was planned in Belgrade and the Bosnian Serb forces took part in it as they had more manpower. However, the special units and the most militant units came from this side. These were police units, the so-called Red Berets. These were special units of the Serbian State Security Service. They were volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party, Arkan's volunteers, and another smaller group of volunteers also under the control of the police. The army was not very involved in this operation. For the most part it provided artillery support where needed. The operation had been planned for a long time. There had been lengthy preparations for it so there were no anxious calls of: Hurry-up, we need this or that urgently. Everything was well organised and carried out until the hostilities ended. Later when looting began, no one was able to control it. "The reporter: Whose idea was it and how well was it prepared? "Vojislav Seselj: This was thought up by key persons from the State Security Service including Franko Simatovic, aka Frenki. And he was one of the persons who carried it out."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, Dr. Seselj -- this ends at 01:07:09.4, the previous clip ended at 00:59:37. So is it correct, Dr. Seselj, that these are examples of some of the aspects of support provided by Mr. Milosevic and his services both in Croatia and Zvornik on behalf of the Serbian efforts there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for you to understand properly what I am talking about here, you would need to read the entire interview and I'm surprised you haven't already. I published the entire interview in one of my books and I forwarded it to The Hague Prosecution in 2003. I forwarded the set of all 80 of my books published by that time. You provided a number of clips here and I'm not sure I remember everything. Firstly, as regards the participation of the Serb Radical Party volunteers in fighting, there were two stages. There was the stage which from the point of view of the then-political and legal system could have been considered illegal. That was the stage up until the Yugoslav People's Army took part in operations. We covertly sent volunteers across the Danube and transported weapons to them. Only during my case when General Pekic died did I reveal that most of the weapons were procured by him in 1991 and that it contained old M48 rifles, the Thompson automatic rifles, and some Russian rifles. The weapons procured were actually to be decommissioned, but he was an influential person, General Dusan Pekic, so he managed to take it over from military warehouses without -- without any problem. Why would I not say that to Laura Silber? At the time we talked my main problem was Milosevic, the main threat was coming from him, and I had a very critical position vis-a-vis his politics. I did not want to refer to Dusan Pekic so that he wouldn't have to bear any consequences in that regard. I protected his name until his death. Now that he is not with us anymore, by mentioning his name I praised his historical role without causing damage. As regards the Serb Radical Party volunteers, all those who were part of the then-authorities in Serbia were full of praise for our volunteers as the most disciplined and bravest. In terms of our volunteers, no one could attach any criminal conduct to their activities and no war crimes. I have been here for 11 years and yet did -- they did not manage to dig up any connection between me and the Serb Radical Party volunteers and specific crimes. That link is not there. Milosevic, of course, had a positive position, he approved the sending of our volunteers. Whether it was precisely the way I explained in the footage or whether I stressed it to a larger measure to annoy him, well I knew what kind of effect it would cause because at that time Milosevic began approaching Western powers and he exercised pressure on the RS government to accept the Contact Group plan. We parted ways with Milosevic as early as 1993 because he accepted the Vance-Owen Plan. That's when we definitely split up. As of 1993 until 1997 we were in fierce conflict, such conflict in which at any point in time I had to think whether I would live through it. I received direct caution from top state security people who told me that my head, my skin, was at risk. I had my own man in the state security. Since he died a few years ago I can say his name, Misan Miletic, he was chief of one of the administrations, and on several occasions he literally saved my life. He told me do not go to this or that place, something was being set out. I was quite well informed and I replied in equal measure or sometime even double that. When I am under attack by the regime, I do not justify myself saying that's not true. I'll give you an example so that you can understand. The current republican president Tomislav Nikolic twice said publicly that from The Hague dungeon I ordered him to be killed which is not true. Had I been in Belgrade I would not have -- I wouldn't have said that's a lie. I would have said: Yes, I did commission his murder and he butchered Croatian grannies in Slavonia. If you justify your position, you lose your argument, but if you retaliate doubly so that steam is coming from the ears of the person who falsely attacked you, then you win in the duel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, although I think you could sense yourself that we were beyond the precise focus of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those excerpts, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. But I note that we don't have access to any transcript that Mr. Tieger was referring to so perhaps he could sort that out in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I hope it to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you and I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it only those shown.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, I wanted to follow-up on something you said on Friday, and that was found at transcript I think 39548 and you referred to the fact that you set out an appeal, an open letter to the Muslims, warning them of threats and appealing to them to avoid the events of World War II when they were instrumentalised by the Croats. So I wanted to turn your attention to a few documents that appear to be related to that. And if we could turn to 25198, please. And let me just show you two documents first and then ask you about those. This first one is an interview on the 31st of May, 1991, first published in Pogledi and then also included in your book Volume 23: "Politics as a Conscientious Challenge." And there at page 2 of the English and 67 of your book, you state --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Politics as a Conscientious Challenge" or "... Challenge to One's Conscience" is not necessarily the best translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So there's a reference to: "We have sent word to Izetbegovic and Cengic to stop playing with their lives and not allow themselves to become a weapon of the Croatian Ustashas again. We told them they should draw some conclusions from the previous wars, because if they let history repeat itself, they should know that, this time, it will be fatal to the Muslims, because us Serbs shall no longer forget or forgive. Our revenge is going to be terrible if the Muslims let themselves become a tool of the Croats." And that was, as I indicated, in May of 1991, the end of May. And if we could also turn to 65 ter 25199 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If you don't mind, I think it's important that he -- his questions be shorter and that he be answering smaller bits because we heard a lot of clips including interesting information about Zvornik, and then by the time the question came around he never really got to answer anything about what had been said in Zvornik because it was so comprehensive what he had seen before he was even asked a question, so I think it's better to break it up so that his answers can be complete and there's no misunderstanding that he's accepted something without having explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to respond to that part of the question that had to do with Zvornik because it seems to me now that you devoted the greatest attention to that but then you stopped me and did not allow me to give a direct answer to that. Do you remember that question about Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- okay, Dr. Seselj, first of all, I have no intention, believe me, of stopping any direct answers to the questions I pose. In fact, I think the struggle has been the opposite. I've actually been endeavouring to encourage you to focus on the questions. So by all means, if you have something more to say about Zvornik, please do so. Similarly, the only reason I'm putting two different passages to you here is because they appear to be quite related and I thought that your response to both would be the same and be assisted by seeing them both. So first Zvornik if you have more to add to that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say anything to you about Zvornik so I have to give a basic answer. There's nothing to add. It is correct that the Zvornik operation was planned in Belgrade and the Serb Radical Party sent about 100 volunteers to participate in that operation. The operation was led by the JNA. This was operations group - now was it the 4th one? - Operations Group Drina and its headquarters was in Gucevo, it's on the right bank of the Drina. Zvornik is a strategically important town. We had information that Muslims there were armed to the teeth, that they had set up paramilitary formations consisting of local criminals, and at one point in time all Serbs had to escape from Zvornik. That's when the JNA decided to intervene and they intervened with the following forces: First, the reserve force of the police in Zvornik itself was mobilised, then they also involved a tank battalion of a brigade that had arrived from Jastrebarsko in Croatia whose commander was Colonel Tacic. Then a special unit of the JNA from Pancevo was involved and its members were Red Berets. You know that at one point in time there whenever people said Red Berets everybody thought Frenki. It was only later that I came to realise that these Red Berets were a military unit from Pancevo. Afterwards, Captain Dragan showed up there in Divic once the fighting was over with some soldiers in uniform who also had red berets. Now, it was convenient for me to attack Frenki at one point given this kind of awareness. However, later on I found out how things exactly evolved. First of all, Arkan came in a police vehicle belonging to the federal MUP and they even had those rotating lights. Also, Arkan was paid to take part in the operation by the Crisis Staff of Zvornik. He's the only one who was paid and he's the only one who entered the operation independently. He was smacked right in the face, sustained certain casualties. I think that happened on the 8th of April, if I remember correctly, and on the afternoon of the very same day the JNA set out with our volunteers and the rest and liberated Zvornik. So I saw things clearly only after a while. This unit, the Yellow Wasps, I said then that it was under the control of the police, but actually later on I saw from documents that it was under the control of the military security services at the outset because Zuca, Vojin Vuckovic, Zuca; his brother Dusan, nicknamed Repic; Milorad Vukovic, Legija; and Miroslav Bogdanovic arrived a day earlier in Zvornik on a mission that General Nedjo Boskovic sent them on to arrest Pusula who was a self-styled Vojvoda who sold weapons to the Muslims. The Muslims captured them, then beat them up, and then they were freed because the Serbs made it possible for a local police official from the Muslim side to escape through Serbia and go to Hungary. That was the precondition. And Zuca's unit was established only after Kula Grad fell. Now, was that on the 23rd of April when the JNA withdrew, when our volunteers had already withdrawn too, Zuca on the spot established that unit and included it in the Territorial Defence and commanded it. This unit was beyond anyone's control and at one point in time they even arrested Brano Grujic, the president of the municipality of Zvornik, and this was totally unlawful. They tied him and carried him through town. Perhaps I've clarified things a bit more for you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to give you that opportunity. Now I wanted to turn back to the document that I had just showed you and, if I may, a document that appears to be related which was 65 ter 25199. Okay. And this was an interview that was with you published in "Der Spiegel" and subsequently published in Tanjug press, and it was dated August 8th, 1991, so it's somewhat after the one we looked at previously. And there we see the following. You were asked -- and this is at page 2 of the English and page 12 of the Serbian. The question was: "Q. You threatened Muslims with revenge if they enter a coalition with Croats. Don't you think that the resistance to Serbian occupation would be expected? "A. Muslims in Bosnia are Islamised Serbs and a part of so-called Croats are Serbs of Catholic religion. Tito forced a million Serbs of Catholic religion and the whole of Yugoslavia to pronounce themselves as Croats after the war. "And if Muslims opposed the attempt to be deprived of a nation status" --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is bad. Bad translation here. Tito forced a million Serb Catholics to declare themselves as Croats, not as Serbs as is written here --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't follow because of the overlapping. Mr. Karadzic, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The interpreters are objecting. They don't see the Serbian page and they can't translate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could we see the B/C/S page, Mr. Tieger? We are not -- I don't think we are on the correct page in terms of B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have it as page 12 and I don't see that as -- and that's what I tried to indicate when I identified the location of that excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's only five pages in e-court in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, sorry, it's also page 2 of the Serbian. So page 2 of the English, page 2 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think you can see it at the upper left-hand portion of the page if that can be enlarged a bit. And I'll just -- and I think what you heard, Dr. Seselj, was because of the problem the interpreters just noted a mistranslation of what I said which basically conformed to what you said; that is, Tito forced a million Serbs of Catholic religion to pronounce themselves as Croats after the war. Then the question was asked: "Q. And if Muslims opposed the attempt to be deprived of a nation status? "A. In that case they will be expelled from Bosnia. "Q. To where." "A. To Anatolia." So these two interviews appear to be your positions at the time regarding the -- something you told us about on Friday, that is, you're threatening the Muslims about what would happen if they sided with the Croats in the dispute with the Serbs; is that correct? Are those, in fact, related to what you told us about on Friday?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, bear in mind that this last interview is not quite authentic. This is an interview I gave to Renata Flottau in the Serbian language. She knew Serbian quite well but not perfectly, so then that was translated into German. Then the Tanjug news agency translated that from German into Serbian. And then now you had this translated from Serbian into English. So this did change the meaning in certain parts. However, what matters and what can be seen from my other speeches and so on directly given in the Serbian language - and that is authentic and you had one such text from Pogledi - that I threatened that terrible things would happen in Bosnia if a war were to break out. Actually, this was a cry on my part. In 1991 I had a big rally in Banja Luka where I also called upon the Muslims not to go to war against the Serbs, that they would suffer the most of all in such a war, and they did suffer the most of all. Out of 100.000 victims, between 60- and 70.000 are Muslims. And these Croats who used them at first for their own interests attacked them from the back in 1993, and I was quite right. This is a year before the war in Bosnia, so what is my objective there? My objective there is to talk Muslims out of a war at all costs, and that meant by saying to them that they should not secede from Yugoslavia because any secession from Yugoslavia would invariably lead to a war. Bosnia and Herzegovina could not secede from Yugoslavia without the Serb people wanting that because the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were a constituent people on the basis of the constitution; that is to say, that without their consent status could not be changed as such. If agreement is reached between Orthodox Catholic and Muslim Serbs that Bosnia-Herzegovina be constituted as a federal unit and that it have three constituent peoples, now all of a sudden two could not join against the third one and say none of that works any longer and off we go. You cannot do it that way. So this was a year before the war. There are some threats in these speeches, but they are calculated threats so that war would be averted. You will not find anywhere that I was the one who wished for a war. I really wished for us to avoid a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina quite sincerely. You can see that from that letter, this appeal to Serbs of the Islamic faith in the beginning of March 1991. You could have found that, it's in the first issue of Velika Srbija and it is part of my case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me tender those, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive them separately.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6389 and P6390 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Seselj, you refer to a possible issue surrounding the "Der Spiegel" article but refer to speeches you'd given. Perhaps then it's useful to turn to 25197 which is a speech of June 4th, I believe, an election campaign speech in Rakovica on June 4th, 1991. And at page 3 of the English and page 64 of the Serbian, again this is another speech that's found in your book, you say the following: "Could the Bosnian pan-Islamists fight a war against us Serbs? Recently we told them: Do not let the Muslim majority become a tool of Croatia like it did in World War I and World War II. Take care, and do not interfere in the Serbo-Croatian conflict. If the Croats use you again, Serbian revenge will be terrible, and you will end up farther than Anatolia, Turkey." And at page 15 of the English and page 74 of the B/C/S we find the following passage: "Us Serbs have forgotten and forgiven too much in history. We have told the Croats should they ever again resort to genocidal activities against the Serbian people, not only shall we take revenge for every victim but we shall also settle scores for the victims from World War I and World War II. However, we have not threatened them yet. We have not attacked a single Croatian village. We have only defended the Serbian villages. If we are not present in some villages or we are unable to defend them, we shall take revenge wherever the Croats are the weakest." And then you conclude: "We speak the language of force, the language of power, because the Serbian people are strong and powerful only when Serbia is united, when the Serbs are united." So it's correct then, if I'm reading this correctly, that the positions that were outlined in the interviews we saw before and which were just admitted were also reflected essentially in contemporaneous speeches you were giving at the time; is that right? Those appear to be essentially the same positions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not fully correct. That's why I drew your attention to the interview that was published in German. If you look at a number of other interviews of mine, it is my claim that the Bosnian pan-Islamists will not stop until Anatolia and not all Muslims, but it was probably easier for the journalist to write Muslims in the context of pan-Islamism. My threat was directed to the pan-Islamists who had assumed the leading role in the Muslim population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as regards the Croats I also threaten to make them desist. It is not our goal to kill all Croats, but it's a warning. Do not play with fire because this might happen. This was what I had been warning of all the time in order to prevent war and not wishing for war. That was the situation when we talk about Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that you admit it in its entirety, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm -- I know the practice has been to admit the relevant pages which -- to which the witness's attention are drawn. I'm certainly content to follow that practice. I'm content either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, unless there's any specific necessity, we'll admit only those pages shown to the witness. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6391, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We looked at an excerpt earlier that described the Serbian lands and what encompassed Serbian lands, and that was during that discussion where we started to talk about Macedonia and then we focused on Bosnia. I wanted to ask you a few more questions about the -- both the scope of what constituted Serbian land in Bosnia and what the basis was. And in that connection I wanted to turn you to a couple of documents that appear to refer to a -- an explanation for identifying what portions of Bosnia might constitute Serbian land. And the first one is 65 ter 25200. This was a television interview conducted on the 6th of December, 1990, for TV Belgrade and it is contained in volume 18 of your book: "The Scythian Disputes." And if we turn to page 8 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S, and let me clarify immediately so there's no confusion that we'll see that this excerpt refers to Croatia and not Bosnia. I'll ask you if the underlying rationale is any different for Bosnia. And here you say the following -- and after indicating that the Serbian Chetniks are constantly telling Tudjman and the authorities in Croatia not to play games with the Serbian people, and then you say: "That is the Serbian territory, populated by the Serbian people, and we shall never allow it to be separated from its mother country. The Croats may separate themselves from Yugoslavia, in other words they may have an independent state, may merge with someone else; however, they must know at all times that at all costs, at the price of new rivers of blood, we shall not let them separate any territory that contains Serbian villages, Serbian mass graves, Serbian slaughter-houses, Serbian pits, Serbian camps, Serbian Jasenovacs, destroyed Serbian churches, we shall never allow that." Now, Dr. Seselj, is it correct that the reference to mass graves, slaughter-houses, camps, Jasenovacs, is a reference to the genocide of World War II and an assertion that in areas where those events took place, those were Serbian areas and could not be under the authority of in this case the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are Serbian territories. Unfortunately, currently they are occupied by Croatia. Croatia was able to occupy them in 1995 with immediate American help. American generals commanded the Storm operation and the Belgrade regime did not move a finger to help the local Serbs and to stop that aggression because the Belgrade regime first and foremost was looking for ways to liberate the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of sanctions. Of course, in 1990 this was my presentation on Serbian Radio Television during the electoral campaign. I ran for the position of president of the republic, and that's when I stated that. In another interview, I spoke about the ways of punishing the Croats for the crimes committed in the Second World War in the way that peoples and states are punished. In other words, not for us to commit a genocide but to punish them by taking territory. I suppose that you found that but it's probably not convenient for you to ask questions about that, Mr. Tieger. And here too I threaten them: Don't do that. But when the war began you won't find me saying anywhere: Go ahead and kill now, go ahead and kill the same way they were killing us. You won't find that in any speech of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm focusing for a moment on the scope of the territorial claims and what constitutes the -- what constitutes Serbian territory and why. So let me ask you it -- was the rationale vis-a-vis Bosnia the same; that is, where crimes of genocide had been committed against Serbs in Bosnia, that that also constituted Serbian land?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you didn't understand my previous answer. The essence is that Serbian lands are in the areas where there is a Serbian majority, and then the accent was put on burnt Serbian villages, expelled Serbian population, Serbian churches, Serbian cemeteries, and so on. All that was on Serbian territory. Jasenovac is Serbian territory because all around it there was Serbian villages. Only in 1995 the area was vacated when the Croats expelled the entire Serbian population of the western parts of Serbian Krajina. It was Serbian, all that, and it will become again one day because this Croatian team cannot last forever. It will be our sons or our grandsons who will achieve that, but we'll never give up on that goal, even if we have to wait for a hundred years. We will reclaim what was Serbian and we will reclaim the Serbian Krajina. In Bosnia-Herzegovina I didn't put forward such positions because the situation was different. In Croatia, apart from Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Serbs, there are also Croats and Slovenians, that is Kajkavians, upon whom Croatian national consciousness was imposed. The original Croats, the Chakavians and Kajkavian Croats, were the ones toward who we had no pretensions. If -- we just wanted for the Serbian lands to remain part of truncated Yugoslavia if they decide to leave. That was part of the programme of the Serbian Radical Party. Not one radical spoke about Greater Serbia at the time. In Bosnia-Herzegovina it's inhabited exclusively by Serbs, over 90 per cent of the population is Serbian as I told you. There may be some Czechs, Poles, Hungarians, Ukrainians, they were mostly made to declare themselves Croatian, but there are also Roma, 5 to 6 per cent. But over 90 per cent are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think you're repeating yourself now. I think you explained that on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I am seeing the clock. We are going to take a break until 11.00. How much longer would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very, very little, Mr. President. I hope -- I mean, I'm loathe to make an estimate, but I can't imagine more than 15 minutes at this point, and I would hope I could conclude sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at two past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if I could tender the relevant page of 65 ter 25200. I believe that's page 8 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll also admit the first page as well. Shall we assign the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6392, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Seselj, one more question about the issue of what standards or underlying principles determined the identification of Serbian territory. And in that regard I'd like to look at a video-clip, and that's found at 65 ter 40628A. The entire speech is at 19:07:00 through 20:36 and this is a clip from that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There are no frontiers between Serbs. The speech of Dr. Vojislav Seselj, president of the Serbian radicals, drew special attention of the visitors. In his speech, Seselj reminded the visitors that Republika Srpska and the republic of Serbian Krajina are the pride of all Serbiandom. The Serbian people west of Drina is a victor on the battle-field but cannot lose the battle at the green negotiating table as their enemies and foreign agents will desire. The people in the Republika Srpska should not be afraid of any threats and the Drina shall never be the border since the Drina is a river running through the centre of Serbia, said Vojislav Seselj. The Drina will never be the border. The Drina is a river running through the centre of Serbia. Muslims and Croats do not represent a threat for us for a long time -- have not represented a threat for us. Only brothers and sister Serbs there shouldn't -- should be no hesitation, no waiting or truce. The next time they strike, we should finish them off so they never strike back."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have an objection about translation. I'd rather speak in Serbian. [Interpretation] The last sentence has not been well translated. Dr. Seselj did not say so they never strike back. He said so that they can never strike, whereas strike back is to return a blow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, I take it since we have the benefit of actually seeing you on screen that that reflected your position about the territory that properly belonged to the Serbs at least with respect to either side of the Drina; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still think and I will continue to think that way as long as I'm alive that the Drina is a river flowing through the heart of Serbia, through the centre of Serbia. It's a central Serbian river. There can be no doubt about that. The existence of an artificial border means nothing. That border cannot be permanent. It's here today and will be gone tomorrow. Nobody can permanently fragment the Serbian people and divide it between countries. Secondly, I here take into account how many truces had been signed with the Croatian federal unit. As long as the Croats are advancing, all doors are open to them. Once they are beaten they suddenly insist on a cease-fire. But there have been no such situations anymore. About Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims strike at the area around Sarajevo, the Serbs launch a counter-offensive and take Igman and Bjelasnica, and Bjelasnica is the dominating mountain in that area. When the Muslims strike from Bihac, they attacked the RS from behind its back which was in 1994. As long as they were advancing, nobody in the west had a headache. When the Serbs in their counter-attack drove back the Muslims to their original positions and when there was a danger of them being totally eliminated as a military factor, then there were threats of bombing, then the ex-US President Carter came to Pale to persuade Dr. Karadzic to stop the offensive and so on. I was always against such tactics. If the war was imposed on us, then we should defeat the enemy in that war. What was bad and the JNA strategy at the beginning of the war was the stop and go, stop and go tactics. That was fatal for the interests of the Serbian people. If war is imposed on us we must defeat the enemy so he can never attack us again, and that obviously means that he must be finished off militarily, but not destroyed as an ethnic or religious or any other group. Here I spoke about militarily defeating the enemy, and if there had been no meddling of Western countries and constant pressures and bombings, then the Muslim army would have been defeated and the Croatian army too and then peace would have been built that would have guaranteed the rights of Orthodox Christians, Catholics, and Muslims equally because we are a historically oriented people. As for the Muslims, they were a privileged class for centuries and they would like to have the same kind of position in an independent Bosnian state because they are a relative majority there. And the Croats have always been the allies of Napoleon, they waged war with him in Russia. Then they were the allies of Hitler, and in the first world war they were the worst criminals in the ranks of the Austro-Hungarian army. They always sided with the most negative forces of the-then world and served their interests. There is no example of the Croats fighting for democracy in all of history. Look at the news of this morning. Magdeburg, the capital of Saxonia, is in danger of being flooded now. You must hear this, Mr. Tieger, it's very important. During the wars in Silesia - you may have heard of them, it's one of the last religious wars in Europe. It was a war between Catholic Austria and Protestant Prussia aided by Sweden. In that war the Croats as a special detachment of Austrian soldiers massacred all of Magdeburg, women, children, every living soul. And there are testimonies of that and you can find that in literature. You can see more about that in my book the "Ideology of Serbian Nationalism." You can see it on my web site and it was published in English too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender that clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, that exhausts my --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be important to give a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date of this speech should be important. I don't know, I mean -- but you should know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not overlap when the others are speaking, Mr. Seselj. Just a second, just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll assign a number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you may proceed about the date, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm only in a position to date it contextually, Dr. Seselj. So by all means if you know a more precise date --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- please feel free to provide it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about a date. I'm interested in you saying it. I think it's important because then we can bear in mind the circumstances under which this speech occurred. Second of all, Mr. Kwon, I understand when you caution me not to overlap with other speakers, but when you at that point in time are being interpreted by the interpreter by raising their voice at me, I don't think it makes any sense. I think interpreters should be emotionless and interpret very flatly. But if you raise the tone, the interpreter raises the tone. I don't see any sense in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters are trying very hard to convey in the words spoken by the interlocutors. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 40, line 21, we can't see who comprised these special detachments of Austrian soldiers. What is missing is that the Croats were in those special detachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That, as I was -- I had begun to indicate, that exhausts my time for cross-examination and that concludes the cross-examination, Mr. President, Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Seselj, today at page 15 of today's transcript you were asked something about Milosevic's assistance. Can you tell us whether the federal state was under an obligation to protect us, the citizens, of the SFRY and to assist us?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was under an obligation but it acted too late. It was too late to react in the territory of the former Croatian federal unit. Had they reacted in time, they could have completely disarmed the units illegally established by Tudjman or, perhaps, to withdraw their forces from Zagreb, Varazdin, and other towns which are objectively speaking Croatian. But on the other side we had a traitor, General Kuzmanovic who handed over an entire garrison in Varazdin with over 150 tanks. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA also hesitated. The war with Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina began as early as 1991. They occupied the area of the so-called western Herzegovina. The line at which they confronted the JNA was the river Neretva, Mostar on one side of the Neretva saw JNA units and on the other side there were paramilitary Croatian formations. It was the basic duty of the JNA to preserve the constitutional order and territorial integrity and sovereignty of the Yugoslav state was much too late in reacting. That is why it was not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 21 you were asked about Zvornik. Can you tell us the date when the SFRY ceased to exist and the FRY was established?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The FRY was established on the 27th of April, 1992, after the second part of the battle which occurred on the 6th or 7th of April and the second part of the battle for Kula Grad on the 23rd of April. That's when things were concluded. However, the JNA had an international obligation to withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina until the 19th of May I think. When the fighting stopped in Zvornik, the JNA withdrew immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know then or do you know now what was my role, my participation in the activities in Zvornik in early April?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had no role to play there at all. You did not have any power to exert any influence. Your party did -- was in power there in coalition with the Muslim parties, the coalition broke up, and your power in the context of JNA activity - I hope you won't hold it against me - but was close to zero. There was a moment I need to mention. Biljana Plavsic who at the time was a member of the Presidency of the RS, I think, came to Zvornik trying to talk the local Crisis Staff into paying Arkan to come to Zvornik from Bijeljina where he had already gone to and with her blessing. You know, Mr. Karadzic, that throughout the war Biljana Plavsic was not being able to be tamed, she led her own isolated policy, and I frequently said that she was not a sane woman and that she should be prevented from appearing in public. I hope you recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was one of the reasons of our disagreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not giving evidence. Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that one of the reasons for our disagreements and did we always agree on everything or only on the most fundamental issues?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic, we did not agree on everything during the war. For example, when you reached an agreement with Mato Boban, president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, when you entered an alliance against the Muslims with him. I came to Pale trying to convince you that we should ask for an alliance with the Muslims against Croats, and I appeared on Radio Pale the same day or the day after and openly in that broadcast I was in favour of an alliance with the Muslims because I believed that in this war too they were manipulated and that it was the issue of survival for both Serbs and Muslims to find a common language. I also knew that at the moment the Croats could not be trusted and that they were only waiting for an opportunity to endanger the Serb Orthodox and Muslim interests. And from today's point of view, I still believe I was not wrong in believing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether we agreed or disagreed with regard to preserving Yugoslavia, with regard to nominating Biljana Plavsic, and several similar issues in which you criticised me, although you did support me in the most fundamental of issues?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no disagreements on the issue of preserving Yugoslavia. I was always more radical and more nationalist in terms of Serbhood than you have ever been. I guess you will acknowledge that. However, we both wanted to preserve Yugoslavia if possible, at least a Rump Yugoslavia, and to avoid war. Our meetings before the war were largely dedicated to that issue. We both wanted to avoid a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As regards Biljana Plavsic, I guess you will remember, Mr. Karadzic, a day in 1996, an entire day, at Koran [phoen] in your residency or office -- it was a large room in any case. I was trying to persuade you. I was there with Tomislav Nikolic, Nikola Poplasen, Mirko Blagojevic, and my close associates trying to persuade you not to nominate Biljana Plavsic on behalf of your party, to run for the president of the republic since you were prevented from running. And I used the same words: She is mad. She will ruin everything and cause much trouble. And yet you wanted her nominated, having in mind that there was a deep rift between her and Milosevic and that Milosevic could not use her against RS, but a mad woman is a mad woman. Not only did she find a common language with Milosevic, but she actually went completely the other way. She became an enemy of Republika Srpska, she ruined it. And then she came to The Hague where she was indicted for war crimes and then she begged, she made agreements, plea agreements with the Prosecution, she was difficult in -- she had difficulty in jail. She had problems with being in -- imprisoned with prostitutes in Sweden. I always thought she was dishonourable and abnormal and amoral and that's why I tried to persuade you unsuccessfully, unfortunately. Since the SDS remained -- stood fast with its decision to have Biljana Plavsic run, we did not propose our candidate in order not to split up the vote of the Serbian people. That year I held over 40 pre-electoral rallies in Republika Srpska and at several such rallies there were always two US security officers from the Sarajevo embassy. They asked for a meeting with me after one of the rallies, perhaps in Teslic. Nikola Poplasen was there as well and someone from the Main Staff of the VRS. Those American officers kept telling me that it would be a good thing for me to run for the RS president since I was born in Sarajevo and they said it would be possible and that I would stand a better chance of winning than Biljana Plavsic. I saw through their ploy, and you can find evidence of it all over, although I had no time to tell you of it. I was talking to them and later at the meeting I said what I had in mind about the -- about Americans, they got their own share right after the meeting with them, until they realised that nothing would come of it. We never wanted to split up the Serbian vote, and that is the only reason why we then supported your candidates. Also, there was something that I held against you very much. During the 40 rallies, we never received any publicity on Serb television, so you, your party too, wanted us to have as little influence over RS citizens in order to get as few votes as we can, as possible, and still we received many.
