So you had the interests of the SDS in mind, whereas I had the interests of the Serb Radical Party in mind, and that was the cause of some friction. However, during the war none of us had any moral right to engage in inter-party conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Despite our mutual respect, when did we run together at some elections in Republika Srpska and Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was late, only in 1998, by which time you were already under the radar, and we had an agreement with the leadership of your party, Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Kalinic, as well as some of my associates, we had a meeting in Loznica where we agreed that our two parties would nominate joint candidates at the forthcoming presidential elections. The deal was that the candidate for the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina would come from your party, Momcilo Krajisnik; the candidate for the president of Republika Srpska, the joint candidate, would be Nikola Poplasen from our party; and the candidate for deputy president or vice-president of Republika Srpska would come from your party, the Serb Democratic Party, Mr. Sarovic. Our coalition received many votes but -- and it was our candidate for the RS president who was elected. Unfortunately, your candidate for a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Krajisnik, was not elected. There was another interesting thing that took place then. A key role in your position was held by Aleksa Buha at the time, former teacher at the school of humanities in Sarajevo who was the minister of foreign affairs, and he tried to convince me that all three candidates should be from your party, yet he was unsuccessful. He became quite upset with your party then and resigned, I believe. From that moment on he was no longer politically active as part of the SDS. So even in your party it didn't go down all too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're on the topic of elections, tell us briefly, how did it happen that Krajisnik lost? Who did he lose to and who did President Milosevic support?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Milosevic supported Zivko Radisic, the leader of the Socialist Party of Republika Srpska. He enjoyed great support of the Serbian media and probably received financial assistance as well. I have no doubt to question that although I do not have specific evidence. That party had better resources, financial resources, than two of our parties together and he won against Krajisnik. Biljana Plavsic was over the top and the Serb people were really fed up with her and they could hardly wait for the next round of elections to be rid of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your then-deputy who is the current Serbian president, Mr. Tomislav Nikolic, together with you, did he have any insight into the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did he have any direct knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did it all together. If I was involved in war crimes, then my direct co-perpetrator or accomplice was Mr. Nikolic, there's no doubt, Mr. Nikolic. But, Mr. Karadzic, I proclaimed him a Chetnik duke in May 1993 and he is preparing to visit Josipovic, the Croatian president, in June in Croatia, and it will be very interesting to see on TV how a Chetnik duke, Mr. Nikolic, is lining up the Croatian Ustasha guards, very interesting. The entire leadership of the Serb Radical Party did its utmost to assist the Serbian people in Republika Srpska and the RSK. Tomislav Nikolic for a month or two was a volunteer in Slavonia. Our general secretary, Aleksandar Vukic, before entering the party was Slavko Aleksic's volunteer at the Jewish cemetery, and then he was withdrawn to work on TV Pale, the Serb TV, because it turned out he was quite skilled in it. And when he returned to Belgrade to try and take whatever exams he had left at the school of law, then he enrolled into our party. So there was no doubt that all members of the Serb Radical Party leadership were very patriotic in their beliefs and that they did their utmost to help the RSK and the RS; that is to say, the Serbs who lived there who fought for their bare survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that we are going a bit too far. I was wondering how this line of questioning arises out of the cross-examination of Mr. Tieger. I just note that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I'm going to drop that subject. But Mr. Tieger referred to this support and these relations between Dr. Seselj and myself, so I wanted to shed full light on all of that because our mutual respect may portray an image of some alliance which came into being only in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In relation to that, Dr. Seselj, between the two of us, was there ever a joint criminal enterprise with the objective of removing Muslims on a lasting basis from our ethnic areas?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no joint criminal enterprise and none of us wanted to remove Muslims on a lasting basis from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I truly suffered and I'm sorry to this day because Muslims were brought into this situation of being manipulated and because there was a war between the Orthodox and the Muslims and the Catholics in Bosnia-Herzegovina. War could have been avoided had Izetbegovic wanted that. Even Milosevic had reached an agreement with Izetbegovic, namely, that Bosnia and Herzegovina remain within a Rump Yugoslavia, that the Muslims have the status of a constituent people in this Rump Yugoslavia, and that Izetbegovic should be the first president of such a Yugoslavia. However, then the Americans persuaded Izetbegovic not to accept that, so it was subsequently that he gave up on this agreement and went into war. There was this Muslim political party called the Muslim Bosniak organisation, I believe, that was headed by Muhamed Filipovic, a member of the academy, and I'm not sure I'm going to remember the name right now, a prominent Muslim emigrant from the communist times who lived in Switzerland, but right now his name escapes me. It doesn't really matter. They understood that it was best for the Muslims to remain in Yugoslavia together with the Serbs because what we Serbs wanted, that is to say for all Serbs to remain within the boundaries of a single state, meant at the same time that all the Muslims would remain within the boundaries of one state. Because if we Serbs are divided up now, so are the Muslims. Because about 100.000 or 200.000 of them live in the area of Raska, the so-called Sandzak; about 100 to 150.000 of them live in Kosovo and Metohija; and 100- or 200.000 in the area of Macedonia, I cannot remember exactly right now; then there quite a few of them left in Montenegro; in Belgrade there are almost 100.000 Muslims, and so on and so forth. So had we remained in a common state we could have agreed on everything together and we could have lived together as equal citizens. There are no language differences among us. We also have a single history irrespective of the different roles we played in that history, and I think that that would have been the best solution. However, unfortunately that solution did not happen. From the west they wanted to have a war, they succeeded in doing that, and that is why everybody fell victim, Serbs and Croats and Muslims. Muslims were the greatest victims, that's for sure, that's a fact. They had to fight against the Orthodox Serbs and those Catholics who called themselves Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there a war of Muslims against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the area of the so-called Cazinska Krajina. There was a war between Fikret Abdic who wanted to preserve Yugoslavia and the followers of Alija Izetbegovic. I think that was called the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that's what the Muslims called their army. And at one point in time this war led to the expulsion of part of the Muslim people through the republic of the Serb Krajina all the way up to Croatia because the 5th Corps managed to take all of the Cazin Krajina. This 5th Corps was receiving supplies from the West and also from the Croats, ammunition, weapons, food, et cetera. Also I have to say that we Serbs assisted Fikret Abdic. Our objective was to have this reasonable option among the Muslims prevail. You know that at the first elections after the fall of communism it was Fikret Abdic who won the majority of the Muslim votes, a lot more than Alija Izetbegovic. And then as a true gentleman he let Alija Izetbegovic become the first president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina because Alija suffered under communism for no reason whatsoever, of course, irrespective of his ideology; and secondly, Alija had a strong political party, the SDA. Abdic as a name was very popular, but he did not have a strong political party that would have followed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If there was no joint criminal enterprise for the Muslims to be removed on a lasting basis from our parts, did you have any knowledge or did you have any views on what the reason was for the major movement of the population during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina from one area to another?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all - how do I put this? - there was this, I should say, natural division of the population. Not a single Orthodox Serb wished to remain in territory that was under Muslim or Croat control. Also, there were quite a few Muslims who wished to remain under Serb control and indeed did so. Serbs, on the other hand, allowed inhabitants of Republika Srpska to live wherever they wished, whereas Muslims forced Serbs to stay on as hostages and would not allow them to leave the territory that was under Muslim control. As a matter of fact, they even forcibly mobilised them into their army and some were also mobilised into these so-called work detachments and sent them to the front line to dig trenches because that is -- it was -- that is where it was easiest to get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you one more thing, in the Serb army there were quite a few Muslims. For example, in Bijeljina I think there were even two brigades consisting of Muslims that took part in the war. They were members of the Army of Republika Srpska if memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These Muslims and Catholics in a Great Serbia, as conceived by you, would they be national minorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. According to our programme, the programme of the Serb Chetnik Movement, the Serb freedom-loving movement which is our name from the 23rd of January, 1990, as far back, then the Serb Radical Party that we established on the 23rd of February, 1991, we have been advocating national unity and brotherly concord between Serb Orthodox, Serb Muslims, Serb Catholics, Serb Protestants, and Serb atheists. So from a religious point of view we have always been very tolerant. The Hague OTP has an enormous number of our documents available and that can be seen on the basis of these documents. No one had the intention of denying anyone any kind of religious freedom. As a matter of fact, I personally was a friend for many years with the Belgrade mufti, Mr. Hamdija Jusufspahic and also we had Sulejman Spaho amongst our ranks for a long time, and he was a member of one of the most famous, glorious Muslim families. And between the two world wars, one of his ancestors established a political party of the Muslims who spoke the Serbian language. Also, another important thing, when King Aleksandar abolished national political parties, when he established the so-called dictatorship of the 6th of January, and then when political parties were renewed, then it was Mehmed Spaho who, together with his Yugoslav Muslim organisation, acceded to the Serb radical community of Milan Stojadinovic; that is to say, there was this Serb Peoples Radical Party, the Yugoslav Muslim organisation, and the Slovene organisation, and they all together comprised the radical alliance. So this is part of the tradition of the Serb radicals, this kind of attitude toward the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in this kind of Greater Serbia -- in this kind of Greater Serbia, there would certainly be some minorities. What would their position be? Could they live as equal citizens in this kind of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our programme documents guarantee full rights and freedoms to the members of national minorities, and within our own political party we had quite a few members of national minorities. We had members of parliament who were ethnic Slovaks, ethnic Hungarians, ethnic Bulgarians, and so on and so forth. I declared an Albanian a Chetnik Vojvoda, Mujo Bunjaku was his name. He took part in the fighting in Mostar in 1992, and he went there under the name of Oliver Denis Baret, but he was an Albanian and a Chetnik Vojvoda later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question, Dr. Seselj, you spoke about language. Do you remember who admitted the Croats into a linguistic union with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your relative, Vuk Karadzic. You hail from the same region, if I remember that correctly. You share the same surname. In 1850 in Vienna a meeting was held between prominent Serb and Croat intellectuals. On the Serb side it was Vuk Karadzic and Djuro Danicic and on the Croat side it was Ivan Mazuranic and a few other prominent intellectuals. Croats at the time did not have a literary language at all. It was agreed then that the Croats would accept the Serbian literary language as their own and that everyone was supposed to work for national unification which actually meant unification of Serb Catholics and Serb Orthodox. However, as soon as they took over the Serb language as their own, the Croats started changing it artificially and this led to an artificial language being spoken in Zagreb today on the basis of the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony, Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Seselj. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the next witness is ready, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oui.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Do you speak French? I shall read it out in French since I am French. I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bataille. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bataille.

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Hello. Yes, good morning to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I provided a statement indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D95272 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bataille, do you see before you the statement that you have given? Do you see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: It is indeed a statement which I have read and which I have signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: This statement overall coincides with what I have said. Overall, that's right with a few details which might be different, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, without any doubt whatsoever. When I'm being asked questions on important subjects, I answer and I don't change my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this statement and these documents be admitted into evidence according to 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you're tendering one associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours the statement 1D25272 will be Exhibit D3669 and 1D25007 will be Exhibit D3670.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Now I'm going to read out a brief summary in the English language. It's a summary of Mr. Yves Bataille's statement. [In English] Yves Bataille is a French academic and author. His wife is Serb -- a Serb and born in Serbia. In 1991, when he owned a book store in Paris, he met Serbs in the diaspora and got interested in the former Yugoslavia as the area became embroiled in the conflict. In about 1992, Mr. Bataille founded the Serbian French association. Mr. Bataille was the president of this association. On 17th and 18th of July, 1995, he met President Karadzic in Pale. They spoke about the position of the French government in particular and the international community in general on Bosnia. During the meeting, Dr. Karadzic received a fax from the United Nations. It indicated that the United Nations had been satisfied with the evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica. Mr. Bataille published this fax in an article he wrote in the "National HEBDO" weekly newspaper at the end of July and the beginning of August 1995. During his meetings with President Karadzic, there was no discussion about prisoners from Srebrenica being been executed. President Karadzic was relaxed during the meetings and gave no indication that there had been any crimes committed in Srebrenica. [Interpretation] That would be the summary. At this point in time, I do not have any questions for Mr. Bataille.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bataille, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, your witness statement. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I see that you have some papers in front of you. Is that your statement or is there something else?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: It's my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Well, and a few notes. Why? What's wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: There is nothing wrong, I just would like to know whether you need to consult with your notes during your testimony or --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: The way you put the question might have implied that there was something wrong. I close the brackets.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No, but if you need to consult your notes, please inform the Chamber and the parties before doing so.

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I don't need to look at my notes, so it's a problem for you and if it is a problem I can set them aside.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, you consider yourself a nationalist; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I'm a Frenchman.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: You have defined yourself as a nationalist to interviews to newspapers; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Well, we should define the term. A nationalist is someone who not only defends his nation but also its sovereignty and independence. And therefore I can define myself as a nationalist according to this definition.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you also consider Dr. Karadzic a Serb hero; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I do think that Radovan Karadzic is a "srpski junak."

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And that means hero?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: It means what you have just said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the same goes for Vojislav Seselj; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Yes, the same goes for Vojislav Seselj, absolutely. And I would like to add something. My testimony will be a testimony regarding facts, regarding things that I have seen, that I have heard, and I have absolutely no hatred or no animosity towards the different parties which were present during the Yugoslav war. I must way that this war was imposed and supplied in a way from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like now to call up your interview which is 65 ter 25120, and in this interview which is dated 15th of November, 2008, you stated - and I'll wait until it comes up, if we could go to page 2 in French and the end of page 3 and beginning of page 4 in English --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: What did I say?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: In the interview you stated that this Tribunal is a new inquisition charged with continuing the war through other means. Is that -- do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. My father was a French magistrate, and he was an advisor at -- for the appeals court of the French republic. And when I showed him a few things about this Tribunal - and let's not forget that this Tribunal was set up by the United Nations, and when I talk about the United Nations, I mean the United Nations and the influence of a small group, and we'll come back to this later on. But coming back to my father, my father told me: This is a legal nonsense. It is a Tribunal that changes its rules, a Tribunal which is supposed to judge conflicts in a country and the Tribunal doesn't know that country, it doesn't know the culture, it doesn't know the mentality apart from a few exceptions. It is very difficult to judge a conflict from a national point of view. So can you imagine at an international level we are talking about an ideology. This Tribunal is put under the influence of an ideology, and this ideology is globalisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you have answered my question. And I would like also to ask you whether you stand by what you said in the same just a little below this first sentence. You say that: "The ICTY is not an independent jurisdiction as it wanted us to believe. This is a Tribunal of convenience financed at the beginning by George Soros and commercial interests, a quasi Tribunal that has conducted and continues to conduct the Anglo-Saxon ritual of politics trials of Serbs whose only crimes was to resist Moloch." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Well, I absolutely stand to what I've said and to what is written, and you have just quoted something that might suit you, but it doesn't bother me at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And in this interview you also praised the association 1389. Did you know that the Serbian prosecutor's office has requested that this association be banned because it spreads national, racial, and religious hatred, bigotry, and active intolerance against minorities, and this is from 65 ter 25115. Did you know that this is a racist association?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I totally disagree with the way you have defined the association 1389, and let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That is not -- that is not my definition. I'm sorry if I interrupt -- that's the definition of --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Well, it's the definition you've just given. But the problem is that you might not know that there is not one association but this is the association 1389 which is the date of the Kosovo battle which was held in 1389, but there are three 1389 associations and not just one. The Serbian government is being pressurised by the "international community," in bracket for international community, because the people who claim to represent the international community do not really represent the international community, but they claim that they do, and the Serb government has threatened. But has it dismantled this association? Do you know this for a fact?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you have -- I believe that your answer is that you do not deem that this association is racist; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: We're talking about a Serb nationalist association. If you introduce some adjectives, you're trying to ruin an association, a group of people. I've asked you a question, Madam, and you never answered my question. I've asked you something. You're talking about this association 1389. I've asked you if it was dismantled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you are here to answer the question, not to ask the question. Please proceed, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I've just been given one of my interviews, it's an interview that I gave some time ago. I'm being told incorrect things. And I think that I'm perfectly entitled to correct what is being said. She's talking about an association. I'm asking her whether the association has been disbanded or not and this is my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely you can clarify whatever you like, but you're not supposed to ask questions to the Prosecutor. Please, let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And apart from meeting with Dr. Karadzic, you also were in touch with Dr. Vojislav Seselj; right? And you helped him get in touch with the leader of the National Front, Jean-Marie Le Pen is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: When I heard that they wanted to meet each other, of course I played the go-between. But this is not an innocent question that you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So I take you did -- your answer is yes, your answer to my question is yes?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I also played the go-between between Brigitte Bardot and an association for the defence of animals in Belgrade. So why aren't you talking to me about Brigitte Bardot. This is not a question on my -- for my part. It's just a comment that I would like to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, I'll ask you questions relevant to this case. That's why I'm not asking you Brigitte Bardot. So you met with Dr. Karadzic for the first time in Pale on the 17th of July, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And he gave you medal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: He gave me a medal, absolutely, and I would like to show you this medal. Here it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Iodice, we didn't hear you because of your overlap with the translation. What -- could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. I asked whether he met with Dr. Karadzic and then I asked whether Dr. Karadzic gave him a medal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 11 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: May I say something about this medal? It is not an award medal. Radovan Karadzic was in his office. He opened up a drawer and here -- there there was this medal which is the angel of Malisevo on one side and on the other side you have the symbol for Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is kindly asked not to overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So because -- for the benefit of the interpretation, could you put a pause between the question and answer. Very well. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So in paragraph 11 of your statement you say that during those two brief meetings that you had with Dr. Karadzic, he did not discuss the executions in Srebrenica with you. In your experience, do people who are involved in mass crimes confess their crimes at first meetings with strangers? Is that your experience?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question because I did not understand your question or it might be a question of translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Did you meet many people who were later accused of committing crimes against humanity or war crimes and mass atrocities?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So you cannot really say whether someone who's accused of such crimes would discuss the commission of these crimes with the -- a stranger, during a first meeting with a stranger; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I must say that this is a very biased question and this is a difficult or unfair question. I see that I cannot talk about my meetings with Radovan Karadzic in his office. We left on the 17th with the driver of Radovan Karadzic. We left the Bosna Vila in Belgrade during the afternoon and we arrived in Pale in the Famos factory which was the building of -- for the government of Republika Srpska. And let me remind you that Radovan Karadzic was the founding father of this republic. I was asked to wait in a room, and after a short while I was taken to his office and I was there in order to assess the situation or to become acquainted with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That was not my question so I'll move on, but if you would please focus on my question. My next question -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. I'm sorry. Please. Then put me or ask me clear questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: You've asked me if I had previously met war criminals. This is what you've asked me. You asked me if I had met war criminals, so I would like to put the terms "war criminals" in brackets because the whole Serb people has been turned into an evil and is now deemed as a collective war criminal. Of course I've met many war corrals. The man of the street, political people, academic people, journalists, and I might be also a war criminal.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Ms. Iodice tell us whether on the 17th of July I was already indicted for the Srebrenica events, as is implied in her question. Her question implies that by that time I had already been indicted for that crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That's not correct I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I'd like to point out I said later accused exactly for that reason. So I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And during the meeting with Dr. Karadzic you received a fax - that's what you say in your statement - you say he received a fax from the United Nations. Was it Dr. Karadzic who told you that that document which is P3997 represented the position of the United Nations on the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I must say that it might be a funny question that you've asked me, it might be funny if we were not in such a context because at the bottom of the document there was the signature of the United Nations -- or you might be talking about another document. I'm talking about a fax that was received and given to me. I must say that I didn't really give it a lot of attention at the time, but when these propaganda or anti-Radovan Karadzic campaign started, anti-Serb campaign started, anti-Serb from Bosnia started, this is when I started paying more attention to the document. This document had been signed by the representative of the United Nations in Srebrenica. It was also signed by the civilian -- the leader of the civilian authorities for the Bosnian people, and it was also signed by a representative of the Serb people. So I guess that this can be seen on the said document.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And I would like to call up P3997.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, do I interpret your answer correctly that you assumed that that was -- that what you saw on that document was the position of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Could I see the document? Could I see the whole document? Can you scroll down or do I do it myself?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see where does it say that it was the position of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be asked not to overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... I see the stamp of the United Nations which is on the left-hand side of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you said just now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see on the left side a United Nations stamp if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Correct. So what I -- my question for you is: Did you assume that that was the position of the United Nations on the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sense is not presented correctly. That's not what the witness said. He said exactly what we can read in paragraph 10. It has to do with the evacuation of civilians, not -- he does not address anyone's position on the Srebrenica events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least that's what I understood. The evacuation of the civilians which unfolded properly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bataille.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Because of your overlap, the interpreters are having a difficult time to hear to interpret your words. I don't think there's much difference, but yes. You can reformulate your question, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, when you saw that fax, did you believe that the United Nations was informing Dr. Karadzic that the evacuation of the civilian population had been carried out correctly?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: My presence in Pale and Republika Srpska was not due to this document. This document was provided to me by chance when it arrived. It is dated 17th of July, the day I was actually there. Now, whether -- well, I did read it afterwards in the evening, and when I returned to France I realised that this document does have the UN stamp on it but also a signature which is that of -- which international organisations are able to recognise. I've got nothing special to say about this document. I came to Pale to see what the situation was like, what the climate was like, and how people were reacting at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sorry, if I --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: This document I --

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. Again, we're straying away from the focus of my question. And -- so I would like to ask you now, when you went back to France you saw what Le Monde and Liberation was publishing at the time, correct, about Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Well, Le Monde and Liberation, you have some interesting references. Le Monde and Liberation and even Le Figaro had been carrying the events in Bosnia for a while already and in an oblique manner. I wasn't born yesterday and I know what propaganda methods are all about, in particular American propaganda methods and public relations organisations that follow the Americans. And it was natural that these media carry "information" which was provided to them, very often wrong information. Since we are on the topic of these newspapers, these same newspapers published the so-called satellite pictures of mass graves in football-pitches. I'll get back to this question later if I have the opportunity to do so. So you are quoting well-known international or French papers, well-known on the international stage, but that changes nothing. You haven't mentioned La Croix. When I returned to France I read an article on Srebrenica based on the -- an ICRC document based in Geneva entitled: "Were there 8.000 dead in Srebrenica?" It so happens that in the days that follow, the figure remained but the question mark disappeared. And what was a question became a statement and a media bombing. Sorry, I graduated from a school of journalism and I know how the media works and I know how the media has evolved over the last few years.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And after you saw those articles you wrote your article that is now Exhibit -- that is number 1D25007 and that's been exhibited with a different number at this stage and -- if you could wait for my question.

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: In this article you referred to the articles you saw in Liberation and Monde, and I would like to show you 65 ter 25228. This is an article from Liberation dated 24th of July, 1995, and recounts the testimony of one of those who escaped from the mass killings in Srebrenica, one of the survivors. Is that one of the articles that you refer to in your article as false?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I probably read this article quickly. Once again, what is written is not written in stone and what I'm concerned about is about deciphering what is written every time there is an important conflict. I would like to say that the Yugoslav war was a laboratory for the wars that followed. In Libya, in Syria at the moment, because the same modus operandi was used and the press --

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, if I could stop you there.

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: -- spreads false news.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That goes beyond my question. So I would like to go back to 1D25007.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please concentrate on answering the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, if I'm to be concentrated, the questions must be clear and accurate, which is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you can't answer the question, just say so. Then Ms. Iodice will ask you again or with some explanation. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, this is your article --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: That's what I asked a while ago. That's what I asked a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: This is your article and in this article you can see that you refer to articles from Liberation and Le Monde, and you say: "If we are to believe Liberation and Le Monde, there were veritable chainsaw massacres in Srebrenica at the beginning of the month."

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Yes, so.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: The article that I have shown you from the 24th of July from Liberation is the article that you refer to in your own article, saying that what is stated in that one is false --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Seemingly, yes. This dates back 18 years. I'm sorry, I don't remember some of the details which seem minor to me. What do you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Do you want me to talk about Marc Semo's article. If you'd like me to, I can. It's interesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Then let's look at the following paragraph where you mention a sea of bodies the article in Le Monde on the 25th of July. So you specifically refer to this article entitled: "Sea of Bodies," from Le Monde, 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And now if we could have in e-court 65 ter 25229, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, this is the article that you specifically mentioned in your --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Yes, so.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: -- article. Is it your evidence that what's stated in this article which is the testimony of a survivor of a massacre is false?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I believe that the content of this article is false. It's not the first time that Le Monde, Liberation, and Le Figaro publish articles written on the spot that attempt to move public opinion and shock public opinion. This is part and parcel of the globalist instruments. You would like me to accept everything that's written here? No. If Bataille, that's me, I don't always accept what's written in the newspapers, that are the newspapers of the aggressors anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And in your article you say that you had the proof that these -- that these events were not happening and the proof was that United Nations fax; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Are you going to spend your time going over what Le Monde said, Marc Semo, and what I wrote myself? I said that there is one document, so why do you want to develop this? I said it was one part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to ask -- I would like to tender the Le Monde article and it might be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that you have more questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Unfortunately, if I could be given another 15 minutes, I would be able to conclude within that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have translation for Le Monde?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No. We'll provide one as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In particular, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just with regard to the time, we don't object to her having additional time, but I think the Prosecution has fallen into a habit of not requesting additional time but taking it for granted, and I think we once again ask them to request additional time before simply assuming it. She's already used more time than she was allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, would you like to add anything, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify this. Mr. Robinson spoke to me about what he considered to be my failure to do so earlier. I told him that I had been about to do so, but the Trial Chamber at that point had urged me to continue. I understood the Trial Chamber to be monitoring the time, so I understood that to be a reference to the fact that I should. And in this case, Ms. Iodice just reached her time. So I mean, I understand Mr. Robinson's point, but I think he's being a bit hyper-technical at this point, and I just wanted to make the broad point the Prosecution is aware of that, and as I told Mr. Robinson, as a normal manner we do monitor it carefully, alert the Court when we've used the allotted time, and request additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will leave it at that. We'll admit this Le Monde article.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6394, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification pending translation. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 20 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, I have very limited time right now, so I would kindly ask you to try and limit your answers to yes and no when possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: If we could have back 1D25007 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir -- and maybe if we could -- thank you. Sir, the fourth paragraph of your article quotes directly from an article from Liberation dated 24th of July. And the article is entitled: "I hid underneath the people who were shot." Do you see that part on your article? It's the fourth paragraph and in French it says [French spoken]. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Yes. So what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: If we could go back to 65 ter -- maybe we could keep the French -- this French translation on one side and on the other side we could go to 65 ter 25228 again.

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Do you mean the fourth paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you could just hold on for a second while I show you another article. Sir, this is the article from Liberation dated 24th of July, 1995, that you directly quote in your article, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I refer to it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: You stand by what you said before about the other article, that you believe that the events narrated in this article from Liberation are false; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Mr. Marc Semo was a journalist working for Liberation and in various conflicts he always writes about the same thing. And here if I understand correctly the person wished to remain anonymous.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So your answer to my question is yes; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Answer to what? In brief --

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: My question to you --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: -- what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: -- was: You believe that what is narrated in this article is false; correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Now, to form an opinion I don't only base this on one single article. You are drawing my attention on one article to avoid focusing on the United Nations article. What is of interest here is the United Nations article.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: We'll get to that. I'm just asking you -- if you let me continue --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Let me continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When did the witness said the content of this article was false?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Of the other article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the other. Not this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That was I understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he talked about the Le Monde.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: At page 72, line 20, he says: "I believe that the content of this article is false."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was referring to Le Monde.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Le Monde, yes, and that's why I'm asking him whether he believes that also the content of this article is false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I misunderstood your question because you asked whether he stood by his statement. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer my question. Do you also believe that the content of this article is false?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: You mean Marc Semo's article? Yes, I believe that this is war propaganda, and I told you a while ago that Marc Semo was used to always writing the same kind of article. He also covered the war of aggression against Libya.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we could go back also to the English translation of 1D25007, your article. In your article at the end you state that the United Nations document that you saw signed by the Muslim representative and bearing the UNPROFOR seal completely invalidates the possibility of there having been massacres, rapes, and disappearances. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: The UN document clearly states that the evacuation of the civilian population went off properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you didn't know, I take, that the United Nations representative who signed that document came here to testify - and I refer Your Honours to Robert Franken's statement at P4175 at paragraph 105 - and he said that the part of the document stating the population can remain in the enclave or evacuate is nonsense. You didn't know that, did you?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. Do you have his statement? Can we see his statement? And in any case, let me tell you: Have you ever heard of Helen Ranta, a forensic Norwegian expert who was an expert and investigated into the Racak operation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: This person was so pressured so much so -- well, this is the same thing. We are talking about the same thing. We're talking about the Yugoslav war.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I understand that there are many things that we could talk about, but, please, you've answered my question, so I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: I will not answer just in one sentence, that is meaningless. I will only answer if I give you the whole context because everything is connected. The same war propaganda methods were used in Bosnia and in Kosovo and I was there. I was in France and I was there on the spot, so I am entitled to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bataille, you are entitled to say that it's part of war propaganda, but the Chamber has the obligation to focus on relevant things. Dr. Ranta or Racak has nothing to do with this trial. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, I also would like to show you now a document that the UN actually sent to Dr. Karadzic, and I would like to call in e-court 65 ter 13645. Sir, this is a letter from the UN centre for human rights to Dr. Karadzic and it's dated 24th of July, 1995. And if we could move to page 2 in English. This is what the UN sent to Karadzic and told him: "I would like to express my deepest concern regarding the recent events in the Srebrenica area which resulted in the forced displacement of some 40.000 individuals. It has been reported that as a result of these events several thousand individuals are unaccounted for and there is fear that many of these have either been killed or detained." You didn't know about this either, did you?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of this?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: Of course I have. Of course I've heard about this, almost every day, and so what? You know, if people repeat a lie, it doesn't make it true. The missing people in Srebrenica - and we do have documents in order to get the cross-references - the people, the missing people in Srebrenica are, as far as I'm concerned, in the mixed column of the 28th Division of the Army of -- of the armija of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslim army, and they were therefore a military target, and this column where there were supposed to be between 15- or 16.000 men, in this column there were about half of the people who were soldiers bearing weapons and they were going -- they were progressing towards the Muslim lines --

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: -- and of course, of course there were losses among these men. So you ask me questions, but I have the feeling that you think that I've only read one article, but please do believe me I have read many, many articles about this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Sir, I have one last question for you. So is it your evidence today that the first fax from the UN that Dr. Karadzic gave you when you met is true, while this other fax from the United Nations is false? Is that your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Wait a minute. I am here and now you are focusing on a fax. I didn't come here in order to talk about this because this is not the most important thing. It just happens that the second fax that you're talking about arrived after. We know very well what pressures are exerted, what pressures are exerted on the United Nations. We know who is leading the United Nations. We know which is the group who wants to protect the famous right of interference of Mr. Kouchner. We know that the responsibility to protect is not a real responsibility in order to protect. There is a permanent war of the same group against independent nations and states. The no-fly zone, for instance, or the no-fly area, when words have a contrary meaning to what they are supposed to mean, then you're totally lost. In Libya there was a no-fly area --

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: YVES BATAILLE
utterances.text: -- and people were allowed to shell it. So now you're talking to me about a United Nations document. There are more than 30.000 documents of the United Nations. You are just showing me the documents that suit your case. The only valid question -- you just want to know whether the first document is false or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions but I would like to ask that both 65 ter 25228 which is the article and this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we don't have any objection to the article, but this document cannot be admitted through this witness. He hasn't commented. He didn't know anything about it. It doesn't contradict his evidence. And if the Prosecution wanted to use it for what appears to be its true purpose, which is to show notice to Dr. Karadzic, it should have called Mr. Mazowiecki or some other witness in its case not to try to use it in an oblique way like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not overlap. Please wait. Is it not contradictory to his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, because this is a letter being sent saying that people are unaccounted for and they fear that many of them have been killed or detained and he's given evidence that, yes, they could have well been unaccounted for but because they were part of a column, so I don't think it's contradictory to his evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document talks about forced displacement and that directly contradicts the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These -- one UN document contradicts another UN document. I am not the representative of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not for you to decide whether it's contradictory or not. Yes, we'll mark for identification the document from Liberation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P6395, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll admit the document -- the UN document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6396.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, Excellency. Just to thank to Mr. Bataille for his effort and willingness to come to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Bataille. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Kovacevic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal context -- in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please pause between my questions and your answers, just as you did when His Excellency, Mr. Kwon spoke, so that all of this would be interpreted. We speak the same language, though, so if we do not pause, not everything will be interpreted. Also, could you please enunciate your sentences slowly. General, sir, did you give my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 1D9550.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the screen before you, do you see that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last page, please, so that the witness could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same as those contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement and the accompanying documents according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're tendering eight associated exhibits, four of which we're asking to be added to our 65 ter list as we hadn't had them at the time the list was filed. Also, I want to apologise to the Chamber because apparently our case manager neglected to put the 65 ter numbers for all of them and substituting the ERN numbers that were in the original statement. He did that in the Serbian version but not in the English version, and I apologise for any inconvenience that may have caused to you or your staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to the associated exhibits I have a couple of matters to deal with. First, the document referred to in para 45, I don't think the witness makes any substantive comment, and as such I do not think that it forms an indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. Likewise, document referred to in para 49, 1D9551, does not form an inseparable part of the statement in the sense that it -- the statement can be fairly understood without the document. So if you -- if the Defence wants to tender those two documents, it should lead live those documents. Otherwise, I ask Ms. Edgerton whether she has any further objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive the statement as well as the six remaining associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement will be Exhibit D3671 and the six associated exhibits will be Exhibits D3672 through to Exhibit D3677 as listed in the 92 ter notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to read out a summary of General Kovacevic's statement in English. [In English] General Dusan Kovacevic joined the JNA in 1965 and from 3rd of January, 1992, he was posted to the command of the 2nd Military District in the Sarajevo garrison. On 19th of January, 1993, he was elected as minister of defence of the Republika Srpska. General Dusan Kovacevic was aware that the leadership of BH, the SDA, and Alija Izetbegovic conducted an intense media campaign aiming to persuade the Muslim people that BH had to be an independent and unitary state. Alija Izetbegovic stated that he was ready to sacrifice peace for the realisation of an independent B&H and, if necessary, he would start war against those who were opposed. Meanwhile, top Muslim and Croatian politicians in BH were instructing their fellow countrymen in their own paramilitary units to attack the JNA barracks and buildings and to use weapons to evict brutally the JNA from BH. In 1992, the Bosnian government used its legal institutions for activities that were illegal at the time, such as the formation of paramilitary units and the systemic attack of Serbs in places where they were in minority population, as was the case in Bosanski Brod, the village of Sijekovac, Kupres, and many other places. Such grave cases gave cause to the Serbian population to respond and self-organise for self-defence, so they set up sentries made up of the local residents to guard their towns and villages. Eventually these evolved into larger units with the establishment size of detachments and brigades. In order to properly equip the army, the HVO and the Army of BH proved to be ready for anything, theft included. In February 1992, Dusan Kovacevic was asked to retrieve some weapons stolen from the arms factory called Bratstvo by the HVO, under the direct command of Zagreb, while only one year earlier Jovan Divjak, a JNA colonel, was arrested for covertly arming an HVO company in the village of Doglodi, near Sarajevo. At the same time, also the BH army started receiving more and more weapons and, in addition, fighters from Arab countries and members of the al-Qaeda were joining the BH army and posing a serious threat to the Serbs and VRS. General Dusan Kovacevic experienced on his own skin the explosion of these feelings of rage. He was in the command of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo when between March and June 1992, the government of BH together with paramilitaries forced blockaded the building and carried out an armed attack, provoking many casualties among members of the JNA. When Alija Izetbegovic agreed to allow the JNA members to leave the building, the JNA column was attacked by a paramilitary formation of Muslims. Unarmed members of the JNA were beaten and killed. A total of 42 members of the JNA were brutally murdered on 2nd and 3rd of May, 1992, in Sarajevo. Between 160 and 190 members of the JNA were captured. Among the killed, there were people of different ethnicities. Together with other survivors, Dusan Kovacevic found refuge in the military hospital in Sarajevo. As a consequence, a false propaganda on Radio Sarajevo instructed civilians and their paramilitary to use all means and weapons in order to target the hospital. Before the attack, the hospital was under the control of the JNA and all the people, regardless of their ethnic background, were given medical treatment. Dusan Kovacevic was fully aware that both the HVO and the Muslims were well armed, since the former received weapons from the Government of Croatia and later from abroad. At the same time, he was also fully aware of the financial problems suffered by the army of the Republika Srpska. In addition to the poor equipment of troops, the VRS needed to be reorganised since local authorities and municipalities were the real decision-makers, while the Supreme Command was kept in the dark of ongoing operations. In order to create a respected legal and effective system, General Dusan Kovacevic as a minister presented his proposal to renew the army at a meeting of the Supreme Command in May 1993. The proposal was formulated in accordance with the advices offered by foreign experts, including people of the UNPROFOR. Nevertheless, all the members of the VRS Main Staff rejected it except for President Karadzic, whose decision to implement his proposal met the firm refusal of the VRS Main Staff. The reorganisation of the army was also a reason to -- of rivalry between Karadzic and Mladic, since Karadzic believed that the army was asking too much and that the budget was unable to support the requests. This was only one of the frequent nasty spats between Karadzic and Mladic, whose main reason for conflict was Mladic's will to take Karadzic's place and become president of the VRS. Despite of the internal rivalries, the objective of the VRS was not to commit any crimes. When crimes have been committed, these were the results of odd individuals' behaviour and were disregarding the official policy of the army. Muslims left Pale voluntarily and on their own initiative. No one was forced to leave and no one pressured or harassed them. When they asked for transport, this was also organised for them. The minister of the interior was instructed by the president of the VRS and the prime minister to protect all citizens regardless of their ethnicity or any other affiliation. Karadzic did everything to find a way out of the crisis, a peaceful solution to the conflict that would satisfy all three ethnic groups. President Karadzic always sought to find a peaceful solution in Bosnia and he did everything for the war to end as soon as possible. [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I will not rely on the two documents which were not made part of the associated exhibits. At this point in time, I have no further questions of General Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kovacevic, as you have just noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its entirety in writing, that is, your written witness statement. And you will be now cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, before you came here to testify today, you've given testimony in 2010 as a Defence witness in the Perisic case; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you gave audio-recorded statements to the Office of the Prosecutor on two separate occasions in 2001 and 2007; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, over the course of our time together, I'm probably going to ask you to confirm some of the things that you said on those previous occasions, but what I'd like to ask you right now is with regard to the statement that you signed on Saturday night with Dr. Karadzic's Defence team, you never actually saw that statement before you came to The Hague, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did not see the statement before my arrival in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did Dr. Karadzic's Defence tell you that the statement was put together from things you had said during these two interviews and your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Additions were made to this statement on the basis of my previous ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Then I want to begin by asking you a quick question about Dobrovoljacka Street and the events there, because in your Perisic testimony you spoke about Dobrovoljacka Street and you said at transcript page 12573: "We were off heading towards the convoy. I saw General MacKenzie standing next to the second APC just standing there and there was this APC in which there were Izetbegovic and General Kukanjac. I saw Colonel Divjak right there who was giving orders to the effect, 'Stop shooting, stop shooting.'" So in the Perisic case you told the court under oath that General Divjak during those events was giving orders for the shooting to stop, but that's not in your statement that you signed for Dr. Karadzic's Defence, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What I said to the Prosecution is correct. Also what I testified to in the Perisic case is true with regard to Dobrovoljacka Street. In the statement I signed, the last which was drafted by Radovan Karadzic's Defence team, my previous statements were not reflected in totality having to do with Dobrovoljacka Street. Colonel Divjak issued orders to cease fire, but only after having been ordered to do so by Alija Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me just stop you right there, General, before you go further. That's not something you know from your own personal observations at that time, is it, because you were racing to a hospital at that moment, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw and heard that in passing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what you heard was General Divjak screaming out, "Don't shoot, don't shoot"; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I saw Colonel Divjak approaching the APC where Izetbegovic was with General Kukanjac. I saw him climb into the APC. I could see that because I was moving towards the APC. I also saw General MacKenzie standing next to the APC. I heard Izetbegovic mentioning the world and what the world would say, and then I watched them and listened to them passing by. I heard Colonel Divjak ordering to cease fire. I moved on towards the military hospital to help the wounded and rescue the dead -- pull out the dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. We might come back to that in a minute. Some things that I noticed you didn't say in your statement for Dr. Karadzic's Defence, you didn't say that before the war you were the commander of the JNA's 744th logistics base which was in Sarajevo and your area of responsibility at that time covered most of Bosnia and Herzegovina; right? That was in your Perisic testimony at transcript page 12533.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. However, no one asked me anything about it later. I mentioned just now that in this statement there are some elements missing from the statements I had previously provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps then you could confirm this for me. When the JNA was reorganised in January 1992, the 744th logistics base then came under the command of General Kukanjac and the 2nd Military District; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was part of the 2nd Military District and under direct command of the 2nd Military District Commander, Lieutenant-General Miladin Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your title in that reorganisation became chief of logistics and technical services for the 2nd Military District; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It is true that I was assistant commander for logistics, the rear, to the 2nd Army District Commander, General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can you also confirm that as part of your job you were integrally involved in the transport of weapons, military equipment, and ammunition from JNA depots in Slovenia and Croatia to JNA depots in Bosnia and also to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I know that during 1991 an agreement was reached between the JNA General Staff in Belgrade and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina to have parts of the manpower, weapons, and military equipment that were being dislocated from Slovenia and Croatia to be deployed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Together with a number of other people from the then-government in Sarajevo, I took part in determining the deployment locations for those units.
